title: Devin 2.0 and the Future of SWE - Scott Wu, Cognition
talk_summary: Scott Wu traces Cognition's Devin through capability tiers over 18 months, arguing the binding constraint shifts every 2-3 months (instruction-following playbooks, then repo snapshots, then cross-file codebase intelligence, then self-testing, then autonomous backlog execution). The concrete mechanisms are playbooks for repeatable step-following, pre-built repo snapshots/VMs, codebase-structure awareness (call hierarchies, language server, git history), and agent self-testing loops.

takeaways.what_they_do: For repetitive migrations they encode an explicit ordered step list the agent must follow exactly, rather than relying on free-form reasoning, because instruction-following was the bottleneck.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we built this system called playbooks where basically you could just outline a very clear set of steps, have it follow each of those step by step

takeaways.technique: Pre-built repo snapshots on clean remote VMs
takeaways.what_they_do: They snapshot a set-up repo state that agents can reload and roll back to, running on a clean remote VM that can execute CI and linters, so each task starts from a known-good environment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: build a snapshot um that that you could start off that you could reload that you could roll back ... having this clean remote VM that could run all these things

takeaways.technique: Structural codebase intelligence over raw text
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of only reading code as text, they feed the agent call hierarchies, language-server data, and git commit history so it can locate and make consistent cross-file changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: understanding call hierarchies, running a language server, uh, is a big deal. you have git commit history which you can look at

takeaways.technique: Agent self-testing loop before delivering a PR
takeaways.what_they_do: For larger tasks the agent must run code locally, decide what to test, and iterate on failures itself before handing back a PR, which they call a higher-context problem than writing the diff.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to know that it is can can test it itself and often the agent actually needs this iterative loop

takeaways.what_they_do: For complex tasks they split into an interactive phase where the agent answers questions and scopes the work, then a hands-off execution phase, rather than one-shot prompting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you would ask a few questions ... explore the codebase with your agent, figure out what has to be done in the task and then set your agent off

takeaways.technique: Explicit confidence gate before autonomous execution
takeaways.what_they_do: Before acting autonomously the agent must judge whether it is confident it understands the task, escalating to a human when it is not, instead of always proceeding.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you have to be able to say, okay, I'm quite sure that this is the task and I'm going to go execute it now versus I don't understand
